summary:
Systematic Investor 298: May 2024 trend update (long equities, short bonds, long dollar and metals) and Kaminski's paper on managed futures ETFs: regulation, growth, use cases and replication versus direct implementation.
ETFs widen access (model portfolios, institutional liquidity buffer), will probably converge toward index-like products, and use fewer liquid markets.
Trend following is behavioural and non-predictive, so AI is unlikely to change it.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you've seen sort of long Equity signals being paired with short fixed income signals as well as long dollar
claims.claim: Trend positioning in 2024 was polarised: long equities, short fixed income (higher for longer) and long dollar, with a February pivot to long energies and precious and base metals and a May reversal of agricultural short signals.
claims.direction: long equities, long dollar, short bonds, long energy and metals

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: short fixed income that's higher for longer and that's been a noisy trade but it has kind of worked and it definitely was a a good position against the equity draw down we saw in April
claims.claim: Short fixed income worked as a hedge against the April equity drawdown within the trend portfolio even though it was noisy.
claims.direction: short bonds gain when inflation and rate fears hit equities

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's almost like kind of a rolling reversals we're kind of seeing different sectors different markets um getting into a little bit of trouble from a trend following perspective but they don't happen all at the same time
claims.claim: Trend reversals were rolling across sectors rather than simultaneous, so index performance looked calm while manager performance differed depending on sector risk allocation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: btp 50 was down 1.14% for the month of May still up 10 and a quarter for the year
claims.claim: CTA indices at end of May 2024: BTOP50 -1.14% month and +10.25% YTD, SG CTA -0.62% and +11.18%, SG Trend -0.79% and +13.41%, short-term traders flat and +3.6%; MSCI World +3.5% in May.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: until 2020 the regulatory framework in the United States was very um opaque and it wasn't as clear
claims.claim: US regulatory changes (the ETF Rule and the derivatives rule) in 2020 opened the door to futures-based ETFs; systematic trend ETF assets grew from about $220m to $1.45bn and non-traditional ETFs from $20bn to $150bn since 2020.
claims.indicator: ETF assets in systematic trend, non-traditional ETFs

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: they like the liquidity profile of an ETF they thought of it as a liquidity buffer something that they could use as sort of a buffer to their existing uh CTA exposures
claims.claim: Institutions use trend ETFs as a liquidity buffer next to their CTA allocations to adjust exposure without redemption paperwork.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's about three 350 through 45 billion only 5% of that allocation is actually in the retail space
claims.claim: Of about $350bn in managed futures only about 5% is retail, so ETFs and model portfolios could broaden access to diversifying return streams.
claims.indicator: managed futures AUM by investor type

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you're going to rebalance it should be based on sort of things have done well and see equities have underperformed
claims.claim: Managed futures should be a strategic allocation rebalanced to target rather than timed; if adding at all, add during drawdowns since managed futures tend to recover on average.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: roughly 286 billion in Assets in two 2021 were in model portfolios um in the United States in June 2023 it's 424
claims.claim: US model portfolio assets grew from $286bn (2021) to $424bn (June 2023); holding managed futures via ETFs in model portfolios builds in strategic allocation and reduces line-item picking and timing of trend.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: look for the last three years in fact in a higher rate environment with some inflation Bond volatility is
claims.claim: In the last three years, with higher rates and inflation, bond volatility is higher and the stock-bond correlation is positive, so 60/40 provides less diversification than in the prior 40 years.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's very unlikely I think that we're going to go back to this zerp world where interest rates are really low and then all you have to do is buy bonds and stocks
claims.claim: A return to zero interest rates, where buying stocks and bonds suffices, is unlikely, so alternatives are a natural choice, and ETF innovation can make them available to retail investors.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you have an ETF you can use that as a liquidity buffer and if you have cash management issues or you want to come in or out of it you can just use that to get to your target
claims.claim: ETF use cases: direct investment, model portfolios and institutional access as a liquid sleeve to adjust total managed futures exposure without redeeming from individual managers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe they just more focus on the return stream they see from the ticker then all the other stuff that we normally have to answer for uh when it comes to due diligence
claims.claim: ETF buyers may do less manager due diligence and rely on the ticker's return stream, and managers will not know their investors, limiting education during drawdowns.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the correlation of the funds that existed started to move much closer to the actual index of institutional funds
claims.claim: In mutual funds, product proliferation first, then consolidation: surviving managed futures mutual funds became about 95% correlated to institutional products, suggesting ETF markets will converge similarly.
claims.indicator: correlation of mutual funds to institutional index
claims.testable: yes - correlation to benchmark by fund

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if we actually think about the best interests of the investors a lot of it that's why we talk about education is is trying to get people to go from bad to
claims.claim: The goal is to move investors from bad to okay: even a modest managed futures allocation via ETF improves diversification versus none; ETFs use fewer, liquid markets (copper, bonds, maybe no cocoa).
claims.testable: partly - ETF vs no allocation simulation

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: replication is backward-looking um it can be slower to react um and it's not necessarily directly implementing risk management
claims.claim: Replication-based ETFs have lower manager-specific risk and look like industry beta but are backward-looking, slower, and inherit managers' risk management; direct implementation uses actual signals and risk rules but reflects one manager's parameters and can deviate from the index.
claims.testable: yes - compare replicators vs trend indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you could have a single replicator risk because of course there is no guarantee that the model that's being used to
claims.claim: A replicator carries single-replicator model risk; the correlation to the target may be less than expected.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you can't trade as many markets um and perhaps you know might not want to use really really fast signals because of you know the the sort of create Redemption process
claims.claim: ETF constraints (fewer markets, slow signals because of creation-redemption) give industry-like exposure but performance diverges from classic CTAs depending on whether trends are in big markets (gold, yen, equities) or idiosyncratic ones.
claims.indicator: ETF market set vs classic CTA 100+ markets
claims.direction: ETFs do well when trends in large markets
claims.conditions: trends concentrated in large liquid markets
claims.testable: yes - compare ETF vs index by market set

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: research needs to drive performance um and thus you need to be putting Research into areas where you can actually provide an edge
claims.claim: Flat-fee ETFs still require research focused on extended markets and differentiated techniques that justify performance fees, because the mutual fund shift pushed managers toward scale versus return.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: products that were more similar to the index that people liked and that have worked have been the persistent products
claims.claim: Managed futures replicator ETFs will probably converge to higher correlation with the index as in mutual funds, though the CTA index is time-varying, so noise is larger.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a normal classical way of doing Trend following will will do well because it's based on human behavior
claims.claim: Classical trend following based on price history will survive AI because it follows human behaviour (over- and under-reaction) rather than predicting; the internet-era claim that equal data kills trend turned out wrong.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: for a market to go from 100 to 200 it still has to go to 105 110 and that's all the stuff that all we need to to know to pick up
claims.claim: A simple trend model would have captured Nvidia's rise because any price move from 100 to 200 passes through intermediate levels, so prediction by AI is not needed.
claims.conditions: asset must be in the portfolio

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's following the themes of what is moving and ask the why later and that strategy's worked for decades
claims.claim: Trend following does not predict and follows whatever themes move, so AI as a predictive tool for the next word or price gives no advantage to a strategy built on not predicting.
